https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-dozens-dea.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JAP1 A Reuters witness saw 50 bodies, many wrapped in mats and traditional cloths, ​lying in the forecourt of a community mosque ahead of their burial Image: Abubakar Imam/REUTERS Advertisement An overloaded boat capsized in a river in Sokoto state in northwestern Nigeria , leaving at least 50 people dead, local authorities confirmed on Thursday. The boat was reportedly carrying people heading to work on farms, but local officials and residents said that at least 40 children were among the casualties. "I can confirm that so far ​around 40 corpses of children have ​been," said Abdulkadir Yusuf, an area manager of the National Inland Waterways Authority, in a statement to the Reuters news agency. One resident, Samaila Garba, said his 13-year-old granddaughter was among the dead. He said he had counted at least 42 bodies of victims, most of them women and children. "During the rainy season, most women and children go to the farm to work," he told the Associated Press. Nigeria boat accident: rescue work underway Dahir Kure, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency in Sokoto state, told the AFP news agency that rescue operations were underway. "We are now at the scene of the boat accident and have begun rescue work," he said. One former local councilor, Ibrahim Musa, described the situation as "bad," adding: "We already buried 46 bodies, and five others have just been brought out of the river." Deadly boat accidents are common in Nigeria , especially during the rainy season, with scores of people dying each year as a result of overloaded boats, poor maintenance or failure to comply with safety regulations. In January, at least 25 people were killed in Yobe state in the northeast of the country in a similar accident. Edited by: Rob Turner Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/09/hout.text: Three people including an airline pilot were killed in attacks on Riyadh's international airport on Thursday, Saudi Arabia said, after Yemen's Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the facility.The Saudi civil aviation authority said two missile attacks on Thursday on the Saudi capital's airport and a Saudia Airlines aircraft there "resulted in the martyrdom of three citizens".The national flag carrier on Friday confirmed the death of the plane's captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami in an incident at King Khalid International Airport, expressing "profound sadness" and "heartfelt condolences," and stating it honoured "his memory with deep respect and appreciation."The missile strikes on Thursday forced diplomats stationed in the Saudi capital to shelter in place and international schools to take safety measures, as explosions echoed across the city.Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, while the airport advised travellers of the "necessity" to contact airlines before their trips.The kingdom's civil defence agency also said "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh. It did not say if there were casualties there or provide details of the damage.Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.The Houthis have also warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.'Crisis in everything'The Houthis, whose heartlands are in Yemen's northwest, had already controlled the capital Sana'a and most of the country's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014.Riyadh's military coalition intervened to support the government the following year.Yet Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces it backs have struggled to contain the Houthis' latest offensive, despite a pushback aimed at recapturing Red Sea territory including the area around the Bab el-Mandeb strait that is crucial to global energy flows.After declaring its counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.But the group formally known as Ansar Allah insists it is holding its territory, and military sources on both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, ordinary civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.In Yemen's Taiz, the Houthis are laying siege to the government-controlled city in the country's west, depriving residents of their main supply route to the government's temporary capital in Aden."There is a crisis in everything: water, gas, vegetables, everything essential", said Taiz resident Um Rian.
